xmldoc.short_description: Write the neutral struct or a plain matrix to a WFDB record.

param_input_item.param_description: the record to write, with or without its .hea extension; name.hea and name.dat are laid down, and name.atr when annotations are carried.
the neutral struct wfdb.read returns, or one built by hand with a signals field.
a plain matrix, one column per signal, taken as physical and quantised with the gain.
the sampling frequency in hertz of a plain matrix.
the signal packing for the whole file: 16 (the default for a plain matrix), 61, 80, 160, 212, 24, 32, 310 or 311. A struct keeps each signal's own format unless this overrides it.
'Physical': true means the samples are physical and are quantised with each signal's gain and baseline; false (the default for a struct from wfdb.read) means they are already raw integers.
'Gain' and 'Baseline', the scaling for a plain matrix, a scalar or one value per signal (gain defaults to 200 adu per unit).
'Leads' and 'Units', the labels and units for a plain matrix, one per signal.

'Segments', write a fixed-layout multi-segment record: the signals are cut into consecutive pieces, each an ordinary record, named by a master header. Give a vector of per-segment frame counts (summing to the record length) or a scalar chunk size; wfdb.read stitches the pieces back into one record.

param_output_item.param_description: what was laid down: name, format, the number of signals, the number of frames and the files written.

description.p: The one writer of the WFDB record format. It lays down a header and a signal file any WFDB tool can read and this module reads back without loss beyond the quantisation; with raw integer samples (the default for a struct from wfdb.read) the round trip is exact.

Every signal is interleaved frame by frame in the one signal file, and the chosen format is the packing of that file: 16 is signed sixteen bits little-endian, 61 the same most significant byte first, 80 and 160 are offset binary (the stored zero is the mid-scale), 212 packs two twelve-bit samples in three bytes, 24 and 32 are three and four byte words, and 310 and 311 pack three ten-bit samples in four bytes. The legacy differential format 8 is not written.

The header stores for each signal its gain and baseline, so a reader turns the raw integers back into physical units, and a checksum, the modulo-65536 sum of the samples, so a file truncated on disk is caught. A plain matrix is taken as physical and quantised by raw = round(samples * gain + baseline); the default gain of 200 adu per unit is the convention of the arrhythmia databases.

With 'Segments' the record is written as a fixed-layout multi-segment record: the same signals cut into consecutive pieces, each piece an ordinary record of its own, and a master header that names the pieces and their lengths. It is what a long recording stored in bounded files is, and wfdb.read stitches it back into the one record that went in. Give a vector of per-segment frame counts that sums to the record length, or a scalar chunk size.

xmldoc.bibliography: Goldberger et al., PhysioBank, PhysioToolkit, and PhysioNet, Circulation 101(23), 2000; Moody and Mark, The impact of the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology 20(3), 2001.
